summary: This document releases IANA-assigned port numbers for NETCONF-related services that have not been used in production networks. Those ports can then be reused.

plainLanguage.summary: Some parking spaces were reserved but never used. This gives them back so others can use them.

subtitle: IANA gives back ports 831, 832 and 833, which were assigned to NETCONF protocols that were never deployed.

tldr.problem: Three NETCONF-related port numbers (831, 832 and 833) stayed assigned to protocols that are not deployed and whose RFCs have been marked Historic.
tldr.mechanism: IANA de-assigns the port numbers for NETCONF over BEEP and NETCONF over SOAP, adds notes to the ports, and keeps the service names.
tldr.outcome: The three port numbers are released for other uses. The RFC knows of no implementations or deployments that rely on them.

today: RFC 9900 is a Proposed Standard. The unit metadata shows no later RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Ports That Were Never Used
sections.content:
The IANA Service Name and Transport Protocol Port Number Registry lists several NETCONF-related assignments: 830 for NETCONF over SSH, 831 for NETCONF over BEEP, 832 for NETCONF over SOAP, 4334 for NETCONF Call Home, and 6513 for NETCONF over TLS.

Three of these (831, 832 and 833) are for protocols that are not deployed, and the relevant RFCs, RFC 4743 and RFC 4744, have been marked Historic. This document de-assigns those port numbers.
sections.plainLanguage: Three reserved spots were for things nobody ever built. They are being handed back.

sections.title: The Registry Changes
sections.content:
For NETCONF over BEEP, the netconf-beep entries on port 831 (tcp and udp) lose their port number and transport. For NETCONF over SOAP, the netconfsoaphttp entries on port 832 and the netconfsoapbeep entries on port 833 (tcp and udp) lose theirs. The references now include RFC 9900.

A note is added to each of the three ports saying it used to be assigned to the respective service but was released by RFC 9900. Following Section 8.2 of RFC 6335, service names are not de-assigned. Only the port numbers are, for better use of scarce resources.
sections.plainLanguage: The name tags stay on the list, but the parking spot numbers are erased and can go to someone new.

sections.title: Operational and Security Notes
sections.content:
There are no known implementations or deployments of protocols that rely on the released ports. Any existing configurations that tie them to the service names netconf-beep and netconfsoaphttp need to be reassessed and updated.

The document describes no protocol, so it introduces no new security vulnerability.
sections.plainLanguage: Nobody was using those spots, so nothing breaks. If someone did write them down somewhere, they should update their notes.
